nodes.name: Wood-ash glazing of proto-porcelain at Deqing
nodes.description: Yin interprets chemical analysis of proto-porcelain sherds from Deqing kiln sites as evidence that potters deliberately applied lime-rich wood ash to vessels, which reacted with the ceramic body during firing to form a glaze. The study lists 12 excavated Shang-period Nanshan sherds and presents glaze analyses for four (NS-1, NS-4, NS-8 and NS-11). The exact preparation of the ash is unresolved; this reconstruction does not establish that every proto-porcelain producer used this method.

date.label: Shang dynasty, c. 1700–1027 BCE
date.basis: Yin identifies the Nanshan samples as Shang in Table 3.1 and gives these broad dynasty bounds in the abstract.

accepted_established_edges.statement: Yin interprets the glaze chemistry of sampled Deqing proto-porcelain, including four Shang-period Nanshan glazes, as evidence of deliberate application of lime-rich wood ash.
accepted_established_edges.scope: The analysed Deqing wares, including four Nanshan glaze samples; functional process relationship, not a claim of transmission or universal use across all proto-porcelain.
accepted_established_edges.caveats: The process is reconstructed from archaeological chemical analysis; how the ash was prepared remains uncertain.

unresolved_edges.statement: Did Watt’s investigation of a Newcomen model lead to his development of separate condensation?
unresolved_edges.scope: Historical development of the separate-condenser arrangement, rather than attachment of a condenser to the Glasgow Newcomen model.
unresolved_edges.caveats: The Glasgow account also draws on Watt’s recollection; the University states there is no evidence a separate condenser was attached to its Newcomen model. The historical development link awaits independently informative corroboration.
